claim: Tetrapod limbs are composed of three modules: the stylopod, zeugopod, and autopod, which are ordered proximally to distally.
source: In general, tetrapod limbs are composed of three modules, the stylopod, zeugopod, and autopod, which are ordered proximally to distally (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the anatomical structure of a mouse limb.

claim: Fish fins are often subdivided into different anatomical modules along the anterior-posterior axis: the propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium.
source: In contrast, fish fins are often subdivided into different anatomical modules along the anterior−posterior axis—the propterygium, mesopterygium, and metapterygium (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the anatomical structure of a bamboo shark pectoral fin.

claim: The autopod (wrist and digits) is the most apparent morphological novelty during the fin-to-limb transition.
source: Although it is still controversial how this different skeletal arrangement compares with the archetypal tetrapod limb, the autopod (wrist and digits) seems to be the most apparent morphological novelty during the fin-to-limb transition (Clack, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clack, 2009, indicating it is based on published literature.

claim: Autopod-specific regulation of Hoxa13 and Hoxd10-13, which control autopod formation, is conserved in non-tetrapod vertebrates.
source: Despite intensive comparative studies of developmental gene regulation, genetic machinery that differs between fins and limbs remains elusive. Instead, several studies revealed that autopod-specific regulation of Hoxa13 and Hoxd10−13, which control autopod formation, is also conserved in non-tetrapod vertebrates (Davis et al., 2007; Freitas et al., 2007; Schneider et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Davis et al., 2007; Freitas et al., 2007; Schneider et al., 2011).

claim: The expression domains of Hoxa13 and Hoxa11 are mutually exclusive in mouse and chick limbs while overlapping in examined fish fin buds.
source: except that the expression domains of Hoxa13 and Hoxa11 are mutually exclusive in mouse and chick limbs while overlapping in examined fish fin buds (note that axolotl limbs also exhibit such fish-like overlap of these expression domains; Ahn and Ho, 2008; Metscher et al., 2005; Sakamoto et al., 2009; Woltering et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Ahn and Ho, 2008; Metscher et al., 2005; Sakamoto et al., 2009; Woltering et al., 2019).

claim: The custom orthology assignment algorithm is more accurate than other methods for Hox and Fgf genes.
source: The quality of the ortholog assignment, which was assessed by examining Hox and Fgf genes, showed that our custom algorithm is more accurate than other methods (Figure 1C; see Materials and Methods and Supplementary file 4 for details).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: Mouse limb buds exhibit two phases of global regulation of Hoxa and Hoxd genes.
source: In mouse limb development, Hoxa and Hoxd genes undergo two phases of global regulation (Deschamps and Duboule, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deschamps and Duboule, 2017.

claim: During the first phase of Hox regulation, Hoxd genes are regulated by an enhancer group located 3' of the entire HoxD cluster, and the Hoxd genes are sequentially upregulated from 3' to 5'.
source: During the first phase, Hoxd genes are regulated by an enhancer group located 3ʹ of the entire HoxD cluster, and the Hoxd genes are sequentially upregulated from 3ʹ to 5ʹ.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hox gene regulation.

claim: The first phase of Hox regulation helps to establish the arm and the forearm.
source: The outcome of this first phase helps to establish the arm and the forearm.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hox gene regulation.

claim: During the second phase of Hox regulation, enhancers located 5' of the HoxD cluster activate expression of Hoxd10 to Hoxd13 in the presumptive autopod region.
source: During the second phase, enhancers located 5ʹ of the HoxD cluster start to activate expression of Hoxd10 to Hoxd13 in the presumptive autopod region (Hoxa genes are regulated in a similar manner; Deschamps and Duboule, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Deschamps and Duboule, 2017.

claim: The expression levels of Hoxd1 to Hoxd8 were highest at E9.5 in mouse limb buds, representing the first phase regulation.
source: As expected, we detected the two phases of Hoxd gene regulation in mouse limb transcriptomes; the expression levels of Hoxd1 to Hoxd8 were highest at E9.5 (the first phase regulation), and Hoxd11 to Hoxd13 were gradually upregulated later (the second phase regulation; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hoxd11 to Hoxd13 were gradually upregulated later in mouse limb buds, representing the second phase regulation.
source: As expected, we detected the two phases of Hoxd gene regulation in mouse limb transcriptomes; the expression levels of Hoxd1 to Hoxd8 were highest at E9.5 (the first phase regulation), and Hoxd11 to Hoxd13 were gradually upregulated later (the second phase regulation; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The expression levels of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 were highest at E10.5 in mouse limb buds, representing the transitional state between the first and second global regulation.
source: Interestingly, the expression levels of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 were highest at E10.5, which probably represents the transitional state between the first and second global regulation (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is observed in the data and interpreted with reference to Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: Bamboo shark fin buds exhibit similar phasic regulation of Hoxa and Hoxd genes as mouse limb buds.
source: As with mouse limb buds, we found similar phasic regulation of Hoxa and Hoxd genes in the bamboo shark fin transcriptome (Figure 1D), suggesting that these transcriptomic data cover comparable developmental stages between the two species at least with respect to Hox gene regulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In mouse limb buds, Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 expression was highest at E11.5, followed by further upregulation of Hoxd13 at E12.5.
source: For example, in mouse limb buds, Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 expression was highest at E11.5, followed by further upregulation of Hoxd13 at E12.5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In bamboo shark fin buds, Hoxd11, Hoxd12, and Hoxd13 reached their peak expression simultaneously at stage 31.
source: In contrast, in bamboo shark fin buds, these three genes reached their peak expression simultaneously at [stage (st)]31 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mouse limb buds at E12.5 exhibit quantitative collinearity of Hoxd genes, where the expression of Hoxd13 is much higher than that of its neighboring Hoxd genes.
source: First, as a confirmation of the previous observation, we also found quantitative collinearity of Hoxd genes in our transcriptome data of mouse limb buds at E12.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Bamboo shark fin buds exhibited no clear relationship between the genomic loci and the expression levels of Hoxd genes at either st31 or st32.
source: However, the bamboo shark fin buds exhibited no clear relationship between the genomic loci and the expression levels of Hoxd genes at either st31 or st32 (Figure 1—figure supplement 7): Hoxd12 expression was highest among its neighbors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Quantitative collinearity is a consequence of the characteristic global regulation of the HoxD cluster in the mouse limb bud.
source: Given that quantitative collinearity is considered to be a consequence of the characteristic global regulation of the HoxD cluster in the mouse limb bud (Montavon et al., 2008), this result suggests that the bamboo shark fin bud may have a different mechanism for Hoxd gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Montavon et al., 2008.

claim: The bamboo shark fin bud may have a different mechanism for Hoxd gene regulation compared to mouse limb buds.
source: Given that quantitative collinearity is considered to be a consequence of the characteristic global regulation of the HoxD cluster in the mouse limb bud (Montavon et al., 2008), this result suggests that the bamboo shark fin bud may have a different mechanism for Hoxd gene regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bamboo shark fin buds lack quantitative collinearity.

claim: Chick limb buds express nearly the same amount of Hoxd13 and Hoxd12 transcripts in the presumptive autopod domains.
source: Interestingly, a recent study also showed that the presumptive autopod domains of chick limb buds express nearly a same amount of Hoxd13 and Hoxd12 transcripts (Yakushiji-Kaminatsui et al., 2018), suggesting that quantitative collinearity is not a universal feature of fins and limbs, rather varies among species.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Yakushiji-Kaminatsui et al., 2018.

claim: Quantitative collinearity is not a universal feature of fins and limbs, but varies among species.
source: Interestingly, a recent study also showed that the presumptive autopod domains of chick limb buds express nearly a same amount of Hoxd13 and Hoxd12 transcripts (Yakushiji-Kaminatsui et al., 2018), suggesting that quantitative collinearity is not a universal feature of fins and limbs, rather varies among species.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different species.

claim: The chondrogenic pathway is at least partially conserved between bamboo shark fin buds and mouse limb buds.
source: As a result, we found that the chondrogenic pathway was at least partially conserved between bambooshark fin buds and mouse limb buds; the expression level of Sox9 and Runx3 (key transcription factors of chondrogenesis; Fowler and Larsson, 2020) increased relatively early, and that of Acan (a cartilage-specific proteoglycan; Fowler and Larsson, 2020) was upregulated later (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Sox9 and Runx3 are key transcription factors of chondrogenesis.
source: the expression level of Sox9 and Runx3 (key transcription factors of chondrogenesis; Fowler and Larsson, 2020) increased relatively early
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fowler and Larsson, 2020.

claim: Acan is a cartilage-specific proteoglycan.
source: that of Acan (a cartilage-specific proteoglycan; Fowler and Larsson, 2020) was upregulated later
evidence: This is stated with reference to Fowler and Larsson, 2020.

claim: A Nog ortholog was not detected in either the fin transcriptome or the genome assembly of the bamboo shark.
source: In contrast, although Nog is known to be expressed in cartilaginous condensations in mouse limb buds (Brunet et al., 1998), we did not detect a Nog ortholog in either the fin transcriptome or the genome assembly of the bamboo shark.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Nog is expressed in cartilaginous condensations in mouse limb buds.
source: In contrast, although Nog is known to be expressed in cartilaginous condensations in mouse limb buds (Brunet et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated with reference to Brunet et al., 1998.

claim: Pax3 was downregulated over developmental time in both bamboo shark fin buds and mouse limb buds.
source: Pax3 (a marker of myogenic precursor cells) was downregulated over developmental time
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transcriptome data.

claim: The MyoD gene family (Myog, Myod1, Myf5) took turns for further differentiation in both bamboo shark fin buds and mouse limb buds.
source: the MyoD gene family (Myog, Myod1, Myf5) took turns for further differentiation (Chal and Pourquié, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transcriptome data with reference to Chal and Pourquié, 2017.

claim: Mouse limb buds showed upregulation of three myosin genes (Myh3, Myh7, Myh8) at E12.5.
source: In contrast, whereas mouse limb buds showed upregulation of three myosin genes (Myh3, Myh7, Myh8) at E12.5, we detected the upregulation of only Myh7 in bamboo shark fin buds.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transcriptome data.

claim: Only Myh7 was upregulated in bamboo shark fin buds, not Myh3 and Myh8.
source: In contrast, whereas mouse limb buds showed upregulation of three myosin genes (Myh3, Myh7, Myh8) at E12.5, we detected the upregulation of only Myh7 in bamboo shark fin buds.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the transcriptome data.

claim: Myh3 and Myh8 were not found in either the transcriptome or the genome assembly of the bamboo shark.
source: Again, we did not find Myh3 and Myh8 in either the transcriptome or the genome assembly of the bamboo shark.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: 6701 genes were significantly expressed in only one of the two species (bamboo shark or mouse).
source: The result showed that 6701 genes were significantly expressed in only one of these species ('Fin-specific' and 'Limb-specific' in Figure 2A; 3284 and 3417 genes, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The fin-specific gene group included And1 and Fgf24, which are known to control only fish fin development.
source: While the fin-specific gene group consisted of many uncharacterized genes, it included ones that are known to control only fish fin development (Fischer et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010), such as And1 (TRINITY_DN62789_c1_g1_i3 in Supplementary data; ortholog of a coelacanth gene, XP_015216565) and Fgf24 (TRINITY_DN92536_c7_g1_i2 in Supplementary data; ortholog of a coelacanth gene, XP_006012032).
evidence: This is stated with references to Fischer et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: And1 is known to control only fish fin development.
source: it included ones that are known to control only fish fin development (Fischer et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010), such as And1
evidence: This is stated with references to Fischer et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Fgf24 is known to control only fish fin development.
source: it included ones that are known to control only fish fin development (Fischer et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010), such as And1 (TRINITY_DN62789_c1_g1_i3 in Supplementary data; ortholog of a coelacanth gene, XP_015216565) and Fgf24
evidence: This is stated with references to Fischer et al., 2003 and Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: The limb-specific gene group included several genes that exhibit abnormal phenotype in the mouse limb, such as Bmp2, Ihh, and Megf8.
source: In the limb-specific gene group, several interesting genes were listed that exhibit abnormal phenotype in the mouse limb (e.g. Bmp2, Ihh, and Megf8).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: 1884 genes were upregulated during late stages of fin/limb development for both species.
source: We also detected 1884 genes that were upregulated during late stages of fin/limb development for both species, including genes that are well known to be expressed later during fin/limb development, such as the autopod-related transcription factors Hoxd13 and Hoxa13 and differentiation markers Col2a1 and Mef2c ('Conserved, late1 and Conserved, late2' in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 5388 genes exhibited heterochronic expression profiles between bamboo shark fin buds and mouse limb buds.
source: Intriguingly, 5388 genes exhibited heterochronic expression profiles; their expression levels were highest during the late stages of mouse limb bud development but were relatively stable expression throughout fin development ('Heterochronic1'; 3178 genes) or decreased during the late stages of fin development ('Heterochronic2'; 2223 genes; see Supplementary file 7 for the full list of genes and annotations).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: Aldh1a2 is upregulated in the interdigital web of mouse limb buds from E11.5.
source: Aldh1a2 is upregulated in the interdigital web of mouse limb buds from E11.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aldh1a2 positively regulates interdigital cell death.
source: Aldh1a2 is upregulated in the interdigital web of mouse limb buds from E11.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and known to positively regulate interdigital cell death (Kuss et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Kuss et al., 2009.

claim: In bamboo shark fin buds, Aldh1a2 expression was initially uniform and was later restricted to the distal edge of fin buds.
source: On the other hand, in bamboo shark fin buds, Aldh1a2 expression was initially uniform and was later restricted to the distal edge of fin buds (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hand2 and Vcan transcripts were upregulated in mouse forelimb buds at E12.5 and downregulated in bamboo shark fin buds at st32.
source: Hand2 and Vcan transcripts were upregulated in mouse forelimb buds at E12.5 and downregulated in bamboo shark fin buds at st32 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Fgf8 expression was high during the early stages of mouse limb buds and was gradually downregulated at later stages.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Fgf8 expression was high during the early stages of limb buds and was gradually downregulated at later stages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In bamboo shark fin buds, Fgf8 was expressed very weakly at st. 27 and st. 27.5 and was upregulated at later stages.
source: In contrast, in bamboo shark fin buds, Fgf8 was expressed very weakly (around 0.1 TPM) at st. 27 and st. 27.5 and was upregulated at later stages.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Late upregulation of Fgf8 was reported in the apical fin fold of zebrafish pectoral fin buds.
source: Indeed, this late upregulation of Fgf8 was also reported in the apical fin fold (roughly equivalent to the AER) of zebrafish pectoral fin buds (Nomura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Nomura et al., 2006.

claim: In the zebrafish pectoral fin bud, Fgf16 and Fgf24 are upregulated earlier than Fgf8.
source: In the zebrafish pectoral fin bud, Fgf16 and Fgf24 are upregulated earlier than Fgf8 (Draper et al., 2003; Nomura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with references to Draper et al., 2003 and Nomura et al., 2006.

claim: Fgf4, Fgf9, and Fgf17 are expressed in the AER and have a redundant function in the mouse limb bud.
source: In addition, Fgf4, Fgf9, and Fgf17 are expressed in the AER and have a redundant function in the mouse limb bud (Mariani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Mariani et al., 2008.

claim: Moderate expression of Fgf9, Fgf16, and Fgf24 were detected in the early stages of bamboo shark fin buds.
source: Therefore, we also examined these other Fgf genes and found that moderate expression of Fgf9, Fgf16, and Fgf24 were detected in the early stages of bamboo shark fin buds (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The overlapping functions of Fgf genes may have allowed subfunctionalization of the signaling molecules of the AER during vertebrate divergence.
source: Although we cannot infer the ancestral state of the expression pattern, the overlapping functions of these genes may have allowed subfunctionalization of the signaling molecules of the AER during vertebrate divergence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different Fgf gene expression patterns.

claim: Mass heterochronic shifts in gene expression were detected between bamboo shark fin buds and mouse forelimb buds.
source: In sum, we detected mass heterochronic shifts in gene expression between bamboo shark fin buds and mouse forelimb buds.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: A mechanism to maintain upregulation of the expression of genes involved in early fin development may have been either gained in the tetrapod lineages or lost in the cartilaginous fish lineages.
source: In particular, a mechanism to maintain upregulation of the expression of genes involved in early fin development may have been either gained in the tetrapod lineages or lost in the cartilaginous fish lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of heterochronic gene expression.

claim: SHH controls growth and asymmetric gene expression along the anterior-posterior axis in tetrapod limbs.
source: In tetrapod limbs, SHH controls growth and asymmetric gene expression along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Previous studies have implied a relatively delayed onset of Shh expression or a short signal duration in developing fins of several elasmobranch species.
source: Although previous studies have repeatedly implied a relatively delayed onset of Shh expression or a short signal duration in developing fins of several elasmobranch species (Dahn et al., 2007; Sakamoto et al., 2009; Yonei-Tamura et al., 2008), there has not been solid evidence to support such a delay due to the lack of systematic gene expression analysis and the poor staging system of these species.
evidence: This is stated with references to Dahn et al., 2007; Sakamoto et al., 2009; Yonei-Tamura et al., 2008.

claim: Shh transcription was present by the earliest stages examined in both bamboo shark fin and mouse limb buds.
source: We first found that Shh transcription was present by the earliest stages examined in both bamboo shark fin and mouse limb buds, and it peaked when the transcription level of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 was highest, suggesting that there was no apparent heterochrony in Shh transcription timing at least between these two species (red rectangles in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Shh transcription peaked when the transcription level of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 was highest in both bamboo shark fin and mouse limb buds.
source: We first found that Shh transcription was present by the earliest stages examined in both bamboo shark fin and mouse limb buds, and it peaked when the transcription level of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 was highest, suggesting that there was no apparent heterochrony in Shh transcription timing at least between these two species (red rectangles in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: There was no apparent heterochrony in Shh transcription timing between bamboo shark fin buds and mouse limb buds.
source: We first found that Shh transcription was present by the earliest stages examined in both bamboo shark fin and mouse limb buds, and it peaked when the transcription level of Hoxd9 and Hoxd10 was highest, suggesting that there was no apparent heterochrony in Shh transcription timing at least between these two species (red rectangles in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: SHH target genes (Ptch1/2, Gli1, Gremlin, and Hand2) showed a relatively extended period of expression in mouse limb buds compared to bamboo shark fin buds.
source: In contrast, SHH target genes, such as Ptch1/2, Gli1, Gremlin, and Hand2 (Vokes et al., 2008), did show a relatively extended period of expression in mouse limb buds as compared with their expression in bamboo shark fin buds.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the RNA-seq data with reference to Vokes et al., 2008.

claim: The expression peak of SHH target genes was concurrent with that of Shh in the bamboo shark fin bud.
source: Namely, whereas the expression peak of SHH target genes was concurrent with that of Shh in the bamboo shark fin bud, these SHH target genes were highly expressed in E11.5 limb buds, which is one day later than the Shh expression peak (yellow rectangles in Figure 3A and B; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for intact TPM values).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: SHH target genes were highly expressed in E11.5 mouse limb buds, which is one day later than the Shh expression peak.
source: Namely, whereas the expression peak of SHH target genes was concurrent with that of Shh in the bamboo shark fin bud, these SHH target genes were highly expressed in E11.5 limb buds, which is one day later than the Shh expression peak (yellow rectangles in Figure 3A and B; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for intact TPM values).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The expression peak of Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 was concurrent with that of SHH target genes in mouse limb buds.
source: This timing difference is also apparent when comparing the expression peak of Hoxd11 and Hoxd12, which was concurrent with that of SHH target genes in mouse limb buds, but came after downregulation of SHH target genes in bamboo shark fin buds (green rectangles in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The expression peak of Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 came after downregulation of SHH target genes in bamboo shark fin buds.
source: This timing difference is also apparent when comparing the expression peak of Hoxd11 and Hoxd12, which was concurrent with that of SHH target genes in mouse limb buds, but came after downregulation of SHH target genes in bamboo shark fin buds (green rectangles in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Mouse limb buds showed a clear expansion of the expression domain of Ptch1 from E10.5 to E11.5.
source: As previously reported (Lewis et al., 2001; Zákány et al., 2004), mouse limb buds showed a clear expansion of the expression domain of Ptch1 (upper panel in Figure 3C) from E10.5 to E11.5, which is accompanied by the anterior extension of the Hoxd12 expression domain (black arrowheads in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C with references to Lewis et al., 2001 and Zákány et al., 2004.

claim: The expansion of Ptch1 expression domain in mouse limb buds is accompanied by the anterior extension of the Hoxd12 expression domain.
source: As previously reported (Lewis et al., 2001; Zákány et al., 2004), mouse limb buds showed a clear expansion of the expression domain of Ptch1 (upper panel in Figure 3C) from E10.5 to E11.5, which is accompanied by the anterior extension of the Hoxd12 expression domain (black arrowheads in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C with references to Lewis et al., 2001 and Zákány et al., 2004.

claim: Ptch1 was expressed in the posterior domain of bamboo shark fin buds at st. 29 but was substantially downregulated by st. 31.
source: In contrast, Ptch1 was expressed in the posterior domain of bamboo shark fin buds at st. 29 (white arrowheads in Figure 3D), but was substantially downregulated by st. 31, whereas the Hoxd12 expression domain extended anteriorly at this stage (black arrowheads in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Hoxd12 expression domain extended anteriorly at st. 31 in bamboo shark fin buds.
source: In contrast, Ptch1 was expressed in the posterior domain of bamboo shark fin buds at st. 29 (white arrowheads in Figure 3D), but was substantially downregulated by st. 31, whereas the Hoxd12 expression domain extended anteriorly at this stage (black arrowheads in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The timing difference in SHH target gene expression represents an interesting difference in the transcriptional regulation of SHH downstream genes between fins and limbs.
source: However, given that this data set captured the similar expression dynamics of HoxA/D clusters between these species (Figure 1D; also see Figure 4C) as well as the differentiation dynamics of myocytes and chondrocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 8), these results quite likely represent an interesting difference in the transcriptional regulation of SHH downstream genes between fins and limbs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the data.

claim: The limb bud at E10.5 and the fin buds at st27.5-30 have a relatively similar expression profile.
source: As a result, four different distance methods that we examined consistently indicated that the limb bud at E10.5 and the fin buds at st27.5–30 tended to have a relatively similar expression profile (Figure 4A for a Euclidean distance measure and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for other types of distance measures).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distance measures shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transcriptomic profile of all the stages of examined fin buds showed the highest similarity to that of E10.5 limb bud.
source: In addition, the transcriptomic profile of all the stages of examined fin buds showed the highest similarity to that of E10.5 limb bud (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distance measures shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mid-stages of limb and fin buds tend to be conserved over 400 million years of evolution.
source: Therefore, the mid-stages of limb and fin buds tend to be conserved over 400 million years of evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the distance measures.

claim: The comparison of only Hox gene expression did not reproduce the hourglass-shaped conservation.
source: We found that the comparison of only Hox gene expression did not reproduce the hourglass-shaped conservation (Figure 4C), suggesting that other mechanisms constrain the middle stage of development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distance measures shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Other mechanisms besides Hox genes constrain the middle stage of development.
source: We found that the comparison of only Hox gene expression did not reproduce the hourglass-shaped conservation (Figure 4C), suggesting that other mechanisms constrain the middle stage of development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hox genes alone do not explain the hourglass pattern.

claim: PC1 distinguished transcriptome data mostly by species differences.
source: The first component, PC1, distinguished transcriptome data mostly by species differences (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PC2 was correlated with the temporal order of mouse limb buds.
source: In contrast, PC2 was correlated with the temporal order of mouse limb buds (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PC3 showed a clearer correlation with the temporal order of bamboo shark fin buds than PC2.
source: PC2 was also weakly correlated with the temporal order of bamboo shark fin buds except at st27 (Figure 4D), but PC3 showed a clearer correlation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: PC1, PC2, and PC3 are mostly sufficient to reproduce the mid-stage conservation.
source: These three components were mostly sufficient to reproduce the mid-stage conservation in Figure 4A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A for the ratio of explained variables and 2B for the Euclidean distance measure).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: The major loadings of PC2 consisted of the conserved late expressed genes and the heterochronically regulated genes.
source: Indeed, the major loadings of PC2 consisted of the conserved late expressed genes (C8) and the heterochronically regulated genes (C9 and C12) identified in Figure 2A (see Table 2 for the top 25 genes of PC2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PCA loadings shown in Table 2.

claim: PC3 consisted of the conserved early genes and the heterochronically regulated genes.
source: Similarly, PC3 consisted of the conserved early genes (a part of C15) and the heterochronically regulated genes (C12 and C13; see Supplementary file 9 for the loadings of PC3 and others)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the PCA analysis.

claim: The presence of heterochronically regulated genes may at least partly contribute to the mid-stage conservation and the distant relationship between the early/late stages of fins and limbs.
source: suggesting that the presence of heterochronically regulated genes may at least partly contribute to the mid-stage conservation and the distant relationship between the early/late stages of fins and limbs.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA analysis.

claim: The mass heterochronic shift in gene expression, at least in part, contributes to the long distances between early- and late-stage expression profiles.
source: These results indicate that the mass heterochronic shift in gene expression, at least in part, contributes to the long distances between early- and late-stage expression profiles (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A relatively low number of stage-associated genes were detected during the middle stages of mouse forelimb and bamboo shark fin development.
source: Consistent with the previous report (EXPANDE Consortium et al., 2017), we detected a relatively low number of stage-associated genes during the middle stages of mouse forelimb and bamboo shark fin development (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C with reference to EXPANDE Consortium et al., 2017.

claim: The number of tissue-associated genes was relatively low at E10.5 in mouse forelimb buds.
source: We counted genes with 1.0 ≥ TPM and 0.65 ≤ entropy and, again, found that the number of tissue-associated genes was relatively low at E10.5 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 3F (note: the text refers to Figure 3F but this appears to be Figure 4F based on context).

claim: There is an inverse correlation between the hourglass-shaped conservation and the number of tissue- and stage-specific genes.
source: Together, these results indicate an inverse correlation between the hourglass-shaped conservation and the number of tissue- and stage-specific genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of stage- and tissue-specific genes.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks covered 10 of 11 known limb enhancers of the HoxA cluster.
source: First, as a positive control, we found that ATAC-seq peaks that were determined by MACS2 peak caller covered 10 of 11 known limb enhancers of the HoxA cluster (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting a high coverage of true regulatory sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATAC-seq data showed relatively high scores for a quality control index, fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP), compared to data from the ENCODE project.
source: Consistently, our ATAC-seq data showed relatively high scores for a quality control index, fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP), as compared with data downloaded from the ENCODE project (Davis et al., 2018; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 5B with reference to Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Evolutionarily conserved sequences were most accessible at E10.5 in mouse forelimb buds.
source: Reinforcing the result of the transcriptome analysis, we found that evolutionarily conserved sequences were most accessible at E10.5 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The OCRs of E10.5 forelimb bud more frequently contained conserved sequences relative to those of other time points.
source: Alignment results for both analyses consistently indicated that the OCRs of E10.5 forelimb bud more frequently contained conserved sequences relative to those of other time points (Figure 5D; see Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B for the absolute counts of conserved sequences).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Activation of conserved gene regulatory sequences may be one of the proximate causes for the hourglass-shaped conservation of fin and limb transcriptome data.
source: Therefore, activation of conserved gene regulatory sequences may be one of the proximate causes for the hourglass-shaped conservation of fin and limb transcriptome data.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that conserved sequences are most accessible at E10.5.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of ATAC-seq peaks resulted in eight clusters (C1-C8).
source: Using one of the three replicates for each stage, we collected the summits of peaks and the surrounding 1400 bp and carried out hierarchical clustering, which resulted in eight clusters (C1–C8; Figure 6A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: E10.5-specific peaks frequently overlapped conserved sequences.
source: Consistent with the above conservation analysis, E10.5-specific peaks frequently overlapped conserved sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the conservation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Stable peaks (C5 and C6) were enriched for the CTCF binding motif.
source: First, it was convincing that stable peaks (C5 and C6) were enriched for the CTCF binding motif both in de novo motif discovery (Figure 6A) and known motif enrichment analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), which is a major regulator of three-dimensional genomic structure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the motif analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: CTCF is a major regulator of three-dimensional genomic structure.
source: which is a major regulator of three-dimensional genomic structure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: E11.5/E12.5-specific peak C3 was enriched for the HOX13 motif.
source: In addition, E11.5/E12.5-specific peak C3 was enriched for the HOX13 motif (Figure 6A), which was consistent with the increase in the expression of 5ʹ Hox genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The enrichment of the HOX13 motif in C3 was consistent with the increase in the expression of 5' Hox genes.
source: In addition, E11.5/E12.5-specific peak C3 was enriched for the HOX13 motif (Figure 6A), which was consistent with the increase in the expression of 5ʹ Hox genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of motif enrichment and gene expression data.

claim: The enrichment of the HOX9 motif in E10.5-specific peaks (C7) was consistent with the peak expression of Hoxd9 and Hoxa9 at E10.5.
source: The enrichment of the HOX9 motif in E10.5-specific peaks (C7) was also consistent with our RNA-seq data, in which Hoxd9 and Hoxa9 expression levels peaked at E10.5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of motif enrichment and gene expression data.

claim: In E10.5-specific peaks (C7), the LHX1-binding motif was ranked at the top of the motif enrichment list.
source: Interestingly, in E10.5-specific peaks (C7), the LHX1-binding motif was ranked at the top of the motif enrichment list
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the motif analysis.

claim: Lhx2, Lhx9, and Lmx1b are required to mediate a signaling feedback loop between ectoderm and mesenchyme in limb development.
source: the closely related transcription factors Lhx2, Lhx9, and Lmx1b are required to mediate a signaling feedback loop between ectoderm and mesenchyme in limb development (Tzchori et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Tzchori et al., 2009.

claim: There is a transitional increase in LHX and HOX9 motifs at E10.5.
source: For a better understanding of the dynamics of transcription factor motifs, we counted the average number of the above detected motifs within the OCRs of each stage, which revealed a transitional increase in LHX and HOX9 motifs at E10.5 and a gradual increase in the motifs detected in C3 over the developmental stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the motif counting analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 (note: the text refers to Figure 6—figure supplement 3 but this appears to be Figure 6—figure supplement 5 based on the figure captions).

claim: The constitutively accessible peaks (C5, C6) were closely located to genes annotated with 'cellular components'.
source: In addition, Gene Ontology (GO) analysis for the peaks in each cluster revealed that the constitutively accessible peaks (C5, C6) were closely located to genes annotated with 'cellular components' (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the GO analysis.

claim: The dynamically regulated peaks (C3, C4, C7, C8) were associated with genes with 'developmental process', 'multicellular organism development', and 'anatomical structure morphogenesis'.
source: Interestingly, the dynamically regulated peaks (C3, C4, C7, C8) were associated with genes with 'developmental process', 'multicellular organism development', and 'anatomical structure morphogenesis' (Supplementary file 11), suggesting that these dynamic OCRs regulate developmental genes.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the GO analysis.

claim: There are E10.5-specific transient OCRs that exhibit evolutionary conservation, the presence of LHX and HOX9 motifs, and a close relation with developmental genes.
source: Together, these results suggest that there are E10.5-specific transient OCRs that exhibit several characteristics including their evolutionary conservation, the presence of LHX and HOX9 motifs and a close relation with developmental genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of conservation, motif enrichment, and GO analysis.

claim: ATAC-seq signals were most increased during the transition from E9.5 to E10.5 in the mouse limb bud.
source: As a result, ATAC-seq signals were most increased during the transition from E9.5 to E10.5 in the mouse limb bud.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the differential ATAC-seq signal analysis.

claim: From E10.5 to E11.5, the total number of decreased and increased signals was highest, indicating that the OCR landscape was most dynamically changing at E10.5.
source: From E10.5 to E11.5, the total number of decreased and increased signals was highest, indicating that the OCR landscape was most dynamically changing at E10.5 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the differential ATAC-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Stage-specific gene regulatory sequences are likely to be most accessible at E10.5.
source: Thus, in contrast to the transcriptome analysis, stage-specific gene regulatory sequences are likely to be most accessible at E10.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the OCR landscape was most dynamically changing at E10.5.

claim: The C7 cluster (E10.5-specific peaks) contained more peaks that did not overlap with those of other cells and tissues.
source: Moreover, by comparing the peaks of each cluster identified above with ATAC-seq peaks of other cells and tissues released by the ENCODE project (Davis et al., 2018; Supplementary file 10 for the full list of cells and tissues), we discovered that the C7 cluster (E10.5-specific peaks) contained more peaks that did not overlap with those of other cells and tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the tissue-specificity analysis with reference to Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Gene regulatory sequences that are accessible only at E10.5 tend to be limb-specific.
source: Again, in contrast to the transcriptome analysis, the data suggest that gene regulatory sequences that are accessible only at E10.5 tend to be limb-specific (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specificity analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: E10.5 forelimb buds have a unique regulatory landscape enriched for evolutionarily conserved stage-specific and tissue-specific OCRs.
source: Taken together, these analyses revealed a unique regulatory landscape of forelimb buds at E10.5, which is enriched for evolutionarily conserved stage-specific and tissue-specific OCRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of conservation, stage-specificity, and tissue-specificity.

claim: A remarkable number of genes that exhibit the highest expression during the late stages of mouse limb bud development are decreased during the late stages of bamboo shark fin development.
source: Our time-series transcriptome data indicated that a remarkable number of genes that exhibit the highest expression during the late stages of mouse limb bud development are decreased during the late stages of bamboo shark fin development (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The mass heterochronic shift may be caused by the later stages of limb development gaining expression of one or a few upstream transcription factor(s) or signaling molecules.
source: The simplest hypothesis for this mass heterochronic shift is that the later stages of limb development gained expression of one or a few upstream transcription factor(s) or signaling molecules that collectively regulate this group of genes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed heterochronic shift.

claim: SHH-independent regulation of its target genes through the GLI3-HOX complex was previously reported.
source: Because SHH-independent regulation of its target genes through the GLI3-HOX complex was previously reported (Chen et al., 2004), the mismatch between the peak expression of Shh and its target genes may be caused by such SHH-independent regulatory mechanisms that are absent in bamboo shark fin development.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Chen et al., 2004.

claim: The mismatch between the peak expression of Shh and its target genes may be caused by SHH-independent regulatory mechanisms that are absent in bamboo shark fin development.
source: Because SHH-independent regulation of its target genes through the GLI3-HOX complex was previously reported (Chen et al., 2004), the mismatch between the peak expression of Shh and its target genes may be caused by such SHH-independent regulatory mechanisms that are absent in bamboo shark fin development.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed mismatch.

claim: Direct and genetic interactions of GLI3 and HOX have a significant impact on autopod formation.
source: Given that direct and genetic interactions of GLI3 and HOX have a significant impact on autopod formation, the emergence of this interaction may be a key component of the mass heterochronic shift and the acquisition of autopod-related developmental regulation in the tetrapod lineages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The emergence of GLI3-HOX interaction may be a key component of the mass heterochronic shift and the acquisition of autopod-related developmental regulation in the tetrapod lineages.
source: Given that direct and genetic interactions of GLI3 and HOX have a significant impact on autopod formation, the emergence of this interaction may be a key component of the mass heterochronic shift and the acquisition of autopod-related developmental regulation in the tetrapod lineages.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: It is possible that the late stages of shark fin development lost SHH-independent gene regulation.
source: However, because we compared only two species, it is equally possible that the late stages of shark fin development lost this SHH-independent gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis.

claim: It is possible that every one of the heterochronic genes independently shifted their expression to the later stages of limb development or to the early stages of shark fin development.
source: Alternatively, given that the evolutionary distance between these two species is >400 million years, it is also possible that every one of these genes independently shifted their expression to the later stages of limb development or to the early stages of shark fin development.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis.

claim: The expression domains of genes that are positively regulated by SHH might have expanded anteriorly during the fin-to-limb transition.
source: Related to the potential changes in regulation of SHH target genes, by analyzing catshark fin buds, we previously proposed that the expression domains of genes that are positively regulated by SHH might have expanded anteriorly during the fin-to-limb transition (Onimaru et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a previously proposed hypothesis with reference to Onimaru et al., 2015.

claim: The anterior expansion of gene expression domains is likely associated with the substantial anatomical changes during the fin-to-limb transition.
source: Nevertheless, our previous study and Woltering et al. commonly suggest that the anterior expansion of gene expression domains is likely associated with the substantial anatomical changes during the fin-to-limb transition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing different studies.

claim: Whether the anterior expansion of SHH-target gene expression is related to the mass heterochronic shifts will be one of the interesting questions to address in the future.
source: Therefore, whether the anterior expansion of SHH-target gene expression is related to the mass heterochronic shifts will be one of the interesting questions to address in the future.
evidence: This is stated as a future research question.

claim: Transcriptomic conservation during the middle of embryonic development has been reported by many groups using different species.
source: Whereas transcriptomic conservation during the middle of embryonic development has been reported by many groups using different species (e.g. Irie and Kuratani, 2011; Kalinka et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated with references to Irie and Kuratani, 2011 and Kalinka et al., 2010.

claim: Analysis of regulatory sequence conservation during embryonic development has been either incomplete or controversial.
source: analysis of regulatory sequence conservation during embryonic development has been either incomplete or controversial.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the literature.

claim: Nord et al., 2013 proposed that regulatory sequences active at E11.5 are exposed by the highest evolutionary constraint.
source: For example, by analyzing histone acetylation marks on several developing organs in mouse embryos, Nord et al., 2013 proposed regulatory sequences active at E11.5 are exposed by the highest evolutionary constraint.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Nord et al., 2013.

claim: Genes expressed at the segmentation stage of zebrafish embryos tended to be surrounded by highly conserved non-coding sequences.
source: Another study showed that genes expressed at the segmentation stage of zebrafish embryos tended to be surrounded by highly conserved non-coding sequences (Piasecka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Piasecka et al., 2013.

claim: There is a conflicting observation that early, instead of middle, embryonic stages tend to be regulated by conserved OCRs.
source: In addition to these studies, there is a conflicting observation that early, instead of middle, embryonic stages tend to be regulated by conserved OCRs (Uesaka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Uesaka et al., 2019.

claim: This study is the first to convincingly show a clear correlation of conservation status between transcriptomic data and OCRs.
source: Therefore, our present study is the first to convincingly show a clear correlation of conservation status between transcriptomic data and OCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Evolutionary constraints on the gene regulatory apparatus are present during the middle stage of fin and limb development.
source: Our results suggest that evolutionary constraints on the gene regulatory apparatus are present during the middle stage of fin and limb development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of conserved OCRs at mid-stages.

claim: Stage- and tissue-specific OCRs were enriched during the conserved period of mid-stage limb development.
source: Interestingly, we found that stage- and tissue-specific OCRs were enriched in this conserved period, during which a relatively low number of stage- and tissue-specific genes were expressed (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mid-stage limb development is enriched for pleiotropic genes controlled by multiple tissue-specific enhancers, including limb-specific ones, rather than by constitutive promoters that often regulate housekeeping genes.
source: These quite contrasting observations imply that the mid-stage limb development is enriched for pleiotropic genes controlled by multiple tissue-specific enhancers, including limb-specific ones, rather than by constitutive promoters that often regulate housekeeping genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrasting observations of OCRs and gene expression.

claim: Complex regulatory sequences that execute spatiotemporally specific transcriptional controls over pleiotropic genes constrain the evolvability of mid-stage limb development, probably due to the vulnerability of complex regulation to genetic mutations.
source: Therefore, we speculate that, at least in the case of limb development, complex regulatory sequences that execute spatiotemporally specific transcriptional controls over pleiotropic genes constrain the evolvability of this particular period of morphogenesis, probably due to the vulnerability of complex regulation to genetic mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the data.

claim: Mass heterochronic shifts of gene expression may have occurred during the fin-to-limb evolution.
source: In particular, comparative transcriptional analyses prompted us to hypothesize that mass heterochronic shifts of gene expression may have occurred during the fin-to-limb evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the transcriptome data.

claim: Both transcriptome and open chromatin data point to an evolutionary constraint during mid-stage limb development, likely owing to gene regulatory complexity.
source: In addition, both transcriptome and open chromatin data point to an evolutionary constraint during mid-stage limb development, likely owing to gene regulatory complexity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined analysis of transcriptome and ATAC-seq data.
